name: Sara Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm one of four developers at Tallow, a fourteen-person startup that builds carbon-tracking dashboards for small factories. My day starts with checking overnight data imports, because a bakery's gas meter feed breaks about once a week. Then I build features end to end, from the database to the charts. I love that the work points at something I care about. What wears me out is that we're always fourteen months from running out of money.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every single day. I have an AI agent open next to my editor and it writes maybe half my first drafts, which I then fix. I've built little helpers that check the meter imports for me. I share a flat with my friend Hana, who's a physiotherapist, and I've got about three months of savings. Not loads, but I'm not someone who panics easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That would be a strange world for me, because I'm already all in. I'd feel a bit silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools were still useful, just oversold, which is true of most tech. Online I'd post something like, turns out the hard part was always the people and the data. I'd still defend using them for the boring bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my real worry wouldn't be AI at all, it would be whether our startup can raise its next round of money. Our investors bought the AI story too, so if that story dies, the next funding round gets harder. Startups like ours could fold even in a quiet world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building at Tallow and keep using the tools for the dull parts. I'd pick up a couple of freelance jobs building dashboards for local charities, so I have money coming in if Tallow closes. And I'd push my savings from three months toward five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a familiar way. Startup life always feels like this. It's the funding I'd think about at 2am, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if Tallow folded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are other developer jobs in the city, so I'd find something, maybe less meaningful. I'd probably end up at a bank or an insurer. That would be fine for rent, and I'd hate it a little bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel silly. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've told everyone the AI tools are the future, including my dad. If it all plateaus, I'd have to admit I got carried away. My dad would enjoy that more than he should.

say: I'd say AI tools are still **useful**, just **oversold** like most tech.
I'd post that the hard part was always the **people and the data**.
think: I privately worry more about **Tallow's funding** than about AI itself.
Investors who bought the AI story might **pull back**, and startups could fold.
do: Keep building **dashboards at Tallow** and using AI for the dull parts.
Take a couple of **freelance jobs** building charity dashboards.
Push savings from three toward **five months**.
feel: She feels a familiar **startup unease** about money, not about robots.
S0.quote: My real worry wouldn't be AI at all, it would be whether our startup can raise its next round of money.
fieldNote: Even with AI flat, her **startup's runway** keeps her uneasy.
She hedges with **freelance work** rather than waiting.
She'd have to admit to her dad she **got carried away**, which stings a little.

steps.text: Keep building Tallow's carbon dashboards with AI for the dull parts
Take two freelance dashboard jobs for local charities
Grow savings from three months toward five

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's pretty much what I think is already happening. So, okay. Let's go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make sure the gains go to workers and the climate, not just shareholders. I'd post guides on how to use the tools well, because I'd want people to keep up, not get left behind. I'd say firms should cut hours before they cut people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well in this one, at least for a while. I'm the person at Tallow who already knows how to get good work out of the agents. The developers who get hurt are the ones who refuse to touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate our data-import checks completely and spend the time on talking to the factory customers. I'd run a lunchtime session for the other three developers on how I work with the agent. And I'd join the new tech workers' network in the city, because someone needs to speak for the people who aren't keeping up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a small worry underneath. I like change. But I know I'm lucky to like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you thinking of when you say the people who aren't keeping up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Matt, our oldest developer, who's forty-eight and hates the tools. He's brilliant at databases. I could see our boss asking why we need Matt, our oldest developer, and that would make me feel sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you speak up for Matt if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd tell our boss Leo that Matt knows things about our data no agent does. I'd also sit with Matt and show him the tools, gently. Both, really.

I'd tell firms to **cut hours** before they cut people.
think: I privately expect to **do well**, since I already know how to direct the agents.
The developers who refuse the tools are the ones who'll be **hurt**.
do: Automate Tallow's **data-import checks** fully and spend the time with customers.
Run a **lunchtime session** teaching the other developers her agent workflow.
Join the city's **tech workers' network** to speak for people falling behind.
feel: She feels mostly **excited**, with a small worry underneath.
She knows she's **lucky** to enjoy change.
S1.quote: I could see our boss asking why we need Matt, our oldest developer, and that would make me feel sick.
fieldNote: She expects to **gain** from this scenario because she's already fluent.
Her worry is for an older colleague, showing her **solidarity** instinct.
She mixes **automation** in her own work with organising for others.

steps.text: Automate Tallow's overnight data-import checks with AI agents
Teach the other three developers her agent workflow at a lunchtime session
Join the city's tech workers' network

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's the one where me being good at AI tools stops mattering. Two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have to move faster than they've ever moved: income support, and public ownership of the big AI systems. I'd say it everywhere. This is too big to leave to five companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, being good at directing AI agents only matters while the agents need directing. If AGI is here in 2028, nobody needs me in the middle. All my work is screen work, so the three years before robots don't help me directly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every spare penny for two years. I'd look hard at solar panel installation, because it's hands-on, it's growing, and it fits what I care about. I'd do the first-year course part-time while still at Tallow, so I'd have a trade by the time AGI lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the first scenario that makes my stomach drop. I'm usually the calm one, and I wouldn't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Solar installation only buys you about three years before robots. Have you thought about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have. Three years on a roof is still three years of rent paid. And by then maybe the policies have caught up. I'd rather be on a roof than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hana about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my flatmate Hana that her physio hands are worth more than my coding brain now. She'd laugh and say she always knew. Then we'd sit down and work out the rent.

say: I'd call for **income support** and **public ownership** of big AI systems.
I'd say this is too big to leave to **five companies**.
think: I privately see my **agent skills** becoming worthless once AGI arrives.
All my work is **screen work**, so the robot delay doesn't protect me.
do: Save **every spare penny** for the two years before AGI.
Start a **part-time solar installation** course while still at Tallow.
Campaign for **public ownership** of the largest AI systems.
feel: She feels **alarmed**, her stomach dropping for the first time.
S2.quote: Being good at directing AI agents only matters while the agents need directing.
fieldNote: Her adaptability doesn't save her here, and she **knows it**.
She picks **solar work** because it's hands-on and matches her climate values.
She accepts that a trade **only buys three years** but sees it as rent paid.

steps.text: Save every spare penny for the next two years
Take a part-time solar installation course while still at Tallow
Campaign for income support and public ownership of AI systems

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I could do something real with five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have just enough time to set this up fairly, so let's be loud now. I'd push for retraining money aimed at green trades. I'd say that if robots are three years behind AI, we should use those years to build things that matter, like insulation and solar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I could get two more good years in software, then a planned move. I'd use AI to help me learn the trade faster, which is a bit funny. My job is gone by 2031, but I'd have three years on roofs after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Tallow for two years and save. I'd do weekend shifts with a local solar installer to learn the work. And I'd start a small side business doing energy dashboards for the installers, which uses what I know from Tallow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a motivated way. Five years is enough to feel like I'm choosing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the side business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it bridges both worlds. Installers need simple software to show customers what they're saving. It might only last until 2031, but it's money and it's contacts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you give up to fit all that in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weekends, mostly. My climbing club goes. Hana would see me less. I'd miss it, but I'd rather be tired now than stuck later.

I'd say we should use the robot gap to build **insulation and solar**.

steps.text: Work weekend shifts with a local solar installer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to have a whole other career first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best chance we've got to do it right: a shorter week, public retraining, and a fund paid for by AI profits. I'd say the climate work needs doing anyway. Let's put people there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd enjoy the next five years a lot. The tools would get better and I'd ride that. Then around year six I'd move into energy work properly, before it gets crowded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at Tallow or a similar climate company and get really good with the tools. I'd put a little each month into a community energy co-op, which feels like investing in my future work too. Around 2031 I'd move into running solar projects, which mixes planning and site work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more curious than scared. Ten years is time for me to be the one moving first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Running projects is partly thinking work, which AGI could do. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But being on site with a crew and a nervous customer is hard to replace until the robots arrive around 2039. I'd be 40 by then and I'd have a lot more saved. That feels like a different problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad he was half right: the tools didn't save my job, they just gave me time to plan. He'd say he never said that. He definitely did.

I'd say the **climate work** needs doing anyway, so put people there.
think: I privately expect to **ride the tools** for five good years.
I'd move into **energy work** around year six, before it gets crowded.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's the one where being adaptable doesn't help me. What would help is public money for green trade training, paid while you learn, and some kind of income floor so people can make the switch without losing their flat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the climate, and for me that's tied up in all of it. If AI makes everything cheaper but burns the planet, none of the job stuff matters much.

headlineQuote: If AI makes everything cheaper but burns the planet, none of the job stuff matters much.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old** full-stack developer at Tallow, a small carbon-tracking startup.
She uses **AI agents daily** and shares a flat with Hana, a physiotherapist, with three months saved.
Her plateau worry is **startup funding**, and she feels she'd thrive in Steady Disruption.
Fast AGI **alarms** her because directing agents stops mattering, so she plans a move into **solar work**.
She blends **progressive politics** with fast personal action.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it's the one where her **adaptability** doesn't help.
whatWouldHelp: Public money for **green trade training**, paid while learning.
An **income floor** so people can switch careers without losing their homes.
